title: YOU SAY YOU LOVE JESUS… BUT WHAT IF THE PERSON YOU REFUSE TO FORGIVE IS REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR HEART?
paragraphs: YOU SAY YOU LOVE JESUS… BUT WHAT IF THE PERSON YOU REFUSE TO FORGIVE IS REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR HEART?

The wound was real. The betrayal was unforgivable in your eyes. But what happens when the Savior who forgave your sins asks you to release the person who sinned against you? This is the uncomfortable truth about forgiveness, grace, justice, and the dangerous difference between loving Jesus with your lips and surrendering your heart to Him.
There is someone whose name can still change the atmosphere inside your chest.
You could be having a perfectly good day.
Laughing. Working. Praying. Worshiping.
Then someone mentions that name.
And suddenly, you're back there.
Back in the conversation that destroyed your trust.
Back in the room where someone made you feel worthless.
Back in the season when you cried yourself to sleep, wondering how someone who claimed to love you could hurt you so deeply.
Maybe it was your father.
Maybe it was your mother.
Maybe it was the spouse who promised forever and then chose someone else.
Maybe it was the friend who knew your deepest secrets and used them against you.
Or maybe, and this is especially painful, it was someone inside the church.
Someone who quoted Scripture.
Someone who lifted their hands during worship.
Someone who called you brother or sister while quietly destroying your reputation.
And now?
You still believe in Jesus.
You still pray.
You still listen to worship music.
You still say, "Lord, I love You."
But there is one sentence you cannot bring yourself to say.
"Lord, I forgive them."
Not because you don't know what the Bible says.
You know.
You've heard the sermons.
You've read the verses.
You've probably even encouraged someone else to forgive.
But they don't know what happened to you.
They didn't hear what was said.
They didn't see what was done.
They weren't there when your entire world collapsed.
And somewhere inside, a question has been quietly growing.
Can I truly love Jesus while deliberately refusing to forgive someone who hurt me?
Before you answer, there's something you need to understand.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that your wound never happened.
But He is asking you to consider what your refusal to forgive is doing to your heart.
And the answer may be more uncomfortable than you expect.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual battle isn't against the person who wounded us.
It's against the bitterness that wants to become our permanent home.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave us there.
Think about Peter.
One day, he approached Jesus with what probably sounded like a generous question.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
Jesus answered:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven."
— Matthew 18:21–22, KJV
Peter thought seven times was generous.
Jesus shattered the calculation.
In the Greek text, Matthew 18:22 uses the expression ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά (heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta).
It is traditionally rendered "seventy times seven," although the Greek expression can also be understood as "seventy-seven times," echoing the language of Genesis 4:24 in the Greek Old Testament.
But the point is not whether you stop at seventy-seven or four hundred ninety.
Jesus was not giving Peter a forgiveness calculator.
He was confronting the human desire to establish a limit beyond which mercy no longer applies.
And then Jesus told a story.
A king wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
One servant owed him ten thousand talents.
An enormous debt.
So enormous that the amount functions in the parable as an almost unimaginable financial obligation.
The servant couldn't pay.
Judgment was approaching.
He fell down and begged for patience.
But the king did something extraordinary.
He didn't merely extend the deadline.
He forgave the debt.
All of it.
The Greek of Matthew 18:27 says:
καὶ τὸ δάνειον ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ
And he forgave him the debt.
That verb, ἀφῆκεν (aphēken), comes from aphiēmi, a word that can mean to release, let go, remit, or forgive, depending on context.
The servant walked away owing nothing.
Imagine that.
A debt he could never repay.
A future he thought was destroyed.
A judgment he could not escape.
And suddenly, mercy.
But then something disturbing happened.
That same servant found another servant who owed him one hundred denarii.
A real debt.
Not imaginary.
Not meaningless.
One hundred denarii represented a significant sum, commonly understood as approximately one hundred days of ordinary labor.
The second servant begged for patience.
Almost the same plea the first servant had made before the king.
But instead of remembering the mercy he had received, the forgiven servant seized the other man and demanded payment.
He refused mercy.
He had received forgiveness beyond calculation, yet withheld forgiveness from someone else.
And when the king discovered what had happened, he confronted him.
"Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?"
— Matthew 18:33, KJV
Read that again.
Not quickly.
Not as a verse you've heard a hundred times.
Read it as though Jesus is speaking to the place in your heart you've been protecting.
Shouldn't the mercy you received have changed the mercy you were willing to give?
Jesus concluded the parable with a severe warning about refusing to forgive from the heart.
This was not a harmless disagreement over personality.
It was a warning about the terrifying contradiction of receiving mercy while becoming merciless.
And here is where the story becomes personal.
We want God to consider the circumstances surrounding our sins.
But we often want Him to ignore the circumstances surrounding the sins committed against us.
When we fall, we say, "Lord, You know my heart."
When someone else falls, we say, "They knew exactly what they were doing."
When we need mercy, we remember grace.
When they need mercy, we remember the evidence.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin demanding that God treat us according to the cross while treating our enemies according to our anger.
But the Gospel will not allow us to separate those two things so comfortably.
Jesus taught us to pray:
"And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
— Matthew 6:12, KJV
Then He made the warning unmistakable:
"For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."
— Matthew 6:14–15, KJV
These are difficult words.
Especially when your pain is not theoretical.
Especially when the person who hurt you has never apologized.
Especially when they seem perfectly happy while you're still trying to rebuild what they destroyed.
But we must not soften Jesus' warning until it means nothing.
And we must not twist it into something Jesus never taught.
Forgiveness does not purchase salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by earning God's acceptance through our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Yet the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
Forgiveness toward others is not the price we pay to make God merciful.
It is one of the fruits of a heart being changed by His mercy.
A persistent, hardened refusal to forgive is therefore spiritually serious.
It is not something to celebrate, defend, or excuse.
But neither should we confuse a wounded believer who is struggling to forgive with someone who has defiantly decided that Jesus has no authority over this part of life.
There is a difference between crying, "Lord, I want to forgive, but I don't know how," and declaring, "Lord, I know what You command, but I refuse."
One is a painful struggle toward obedience.
The other is resistance to the Lord we claim to follow.
And if you are struggling right now, listen carefully.
The fact that forgiveness is difficult does not mean your faith is fake.
It may mean the wound was deep.
It may mean the betrayal was devastating.
It may mean healing will require time, prayer, wise counsel, and repeated acts of surrender.
Jesus knows the difference between a heart that is bleeding and a heart that is deliberately hardening.
He is not indifferent to either.
But He does not abandon the wounded heart.
He invites it to come closer.
And perhaps this is where we need to confront one of the most dangerous misunderstandings in Christian life.
Some people hear the word forgiveness and immediately think it means letting an abuser back into their home.
Returning to a dangerous relationship.
Trusting a person who has repeatedly lied.
Remaining silent about criminal behavior.
Pretending that the past never happened.
Or accepting the same destructive treatment over and over again.
That is not what biblical forgiveness requires.
Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
Forgiveness is not the same as restored trust.
Forgiveness is not the same as removing consequences.
Forgiveness is not the same as declaring someone innocent.
You can forgive someone and still establish firm boundaries.
You can forgive someone and still report abuse to the proper authorities.
You can forgive someone and still refuse to return to an unsafe environment.
You can forgive someone and still acknowledge that rebuilding trust requires genuine repentance, accountability, and changed behavior.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always achievable through one person's willingness.
You cannot force someone else to repent.
You cannot make someone trustworthy.
You cannot single-handedly restore a relationship that another person continues to destroy.
And forgiveness does not require you to surrender your safety to prove your spirituality.
In fact, Scripture also teaches that governing authorities have a responsibility to address wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4).
Mercy and justice are not enemies.
The God who commands forgiveness also loves righteousness.
And that matters because someone reading this has been told that being a good Christian means remaining available to the person who keeps hurting them.
No.
Jesus never commanded you to call evil good.
He calls you to release personal vengeance without surrendering truth, wisdom, or justice.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
Forgiveness does not mean that evil no longer matters.
It means you refuse to make personal revenge the ruler of your life.
You place judgment into hands more righteous than your own.
And sometimes that surrender happens while tears are still falling.
Now imagine something.
Imagine the person who hurt you never apologizes.
Never acknowledges the damage.
Never tells the truth about what happened.
Never returns what was stolen.
Never admits they were wrong.
Would you still be willing to begin forgiving them?
That question hurts because many of us have attached forgiveness to a future moment that may never arrive.
"I'll forgive them when they admit it."
"I'll forgive them when they suffer like I suffered."
"I'll forgive them when they finally understand what they did."
But what if they never do?
Will your obedience to Jesus remain imprisoned inside another person's unwillingness to repent?
Will their silence decide how long bitterness is allowed to govern your heart?
You cannot control whether they repent.
You cannot control whether they apologize.
You cannot control whether they change.
But by God's grace, you can begin surrendering your claim to personal vengeance.
That does not instantly erase the pain.
It does not guarantee that you will never feel angry again.
It does not mean every memory will stop hurting.
Sometimes forgiveness is a decision you must return to when the wound is remembered.
Not because Christ's command has changed.
But because the human heart often needs to bring the same suffering before Him again and again.
And this is where another Scripture becomes deeply important.
"Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
— Ephesians 4:26, KJV
The Bible does not pretend that anger itself is always sinful.
Some anger is a morally appropriate response to genuine evil.
Even Jesus displayed righteous anger.
But anger can become destructive when we nurture it into resentment, revenge, contempt, or hatred.
Paul continues:
"And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption."
— Ephesians 4:30, KJV
Then he writes:
— Ephesians 4:31–32, KJV
In the Greek, the expression for forgiving one another uses χαριζόμενοι (charizomenoi), from charizomai.
It carries the sense of showing grace or freely granting forgiveness.
It is related to χάρις (charis), the Greek word commonly translated as grace.
That connection is beautiful.
Paul does not merely tell Christians to suppress their anger and act pleasant.
He calls them to extend grace because they themselves have received grace in Christ.
And notice the order.
God's forgiveness in Christ becomes the foundation for our forgiveness toward others.
We do not manufacture mercy from an empty heart.
We draw upon the mercy that has already met us in Jesus.
And perhaps the reason this feels impossible is because you've been trying to forgive through your own emotional strength.
You've been waiting until you feel ready.
Waiting until the memories stop hurting.
Waiting until your heart becomes soft enough.
But forgiveness is not always born from a sudden change of feeling.
Sometimes it begins with a trembling prayer.
"Jesus, I cannot do this without You."
And that prayer may be the most honest thing you've said in months.
Because the Gospel is not a story about strong people saving themselves.
It is the story of a Savior who comes for people who cannot rescue their own hearts.
Look at the cross.
Not the polished version we place on walls.
Not the beautiful jewelry we wear around our necks.
Look at what actually happened.
Jesus was betrayed.
Abandoned.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God suffered at the hands of sinners.
And while He hung upon the cross, Luke records these words:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, KJV
There is a textual detail worth understanding here.

This saying appears in the traditional text of Luke and in many ancient manuscripts, but it is absent from some other early witnesses. For that reason, modern translations sometimes include a textual note.
Christians should be honest about such manuscript questions rather than pretending they do not exist.
Yet the portrait of Jesus extending mercy to enemies is consistent with His teaching and with the wider witness of Scripture.
In the Greek text containing this saying, the prayer begins:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς
Pater, aphes autois.
"Father, forgive them."
Consider the weight of that prayer.
Jesus did not say that crucifixion was acceptable.
He did not declare the violence righteous.
He did not deny the evil being committed.
He entrusted Himself to His Father.
And He prayed for mercy.
But we must understand something else.
Jesus' prayer does not mean every person involved was automatically reconciled to God without repentance and faith.
The New Testament still calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
At Pentecost, Peter confronted those implicated in Jesus' death and called them to repentance (Acts 2:36–38).
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Forgiveness is not God's declaration that sin doesn't matter.
Forgiveness is costly precisely because sin matters.
And nowhere is that cost clearer than at Calvary.
Now here is a question that should humble every one of us.
What if Jesus had treated us according to the standard of mercy we sometimes reserve for others?
What if He said:
"I will forgive you only when you've suffered enough."
"I will forgive you only when you can prove you will never fail again."
"I will forgive you only when your repentance becomes impressive enough to deserve My attention."
Where would we be?
Because the truth is, none of us approached the cross as innocent people.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
The betrayed and the betrayer.
The wounded and the one who wounded.
The religious and the rebellious.
The person who seems respectable and the person whose sins became public.
That does not mean all sins cause equal harm or deserve identical earthly consequences.
It means every human being needs the mercy of God.
And the ground at the foot of the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
Some of us have never committed the particular sin that wounded us.
But none of us can claim we have never needed forgiveness.
This is why Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant is so devastating.
The servant did not misunderstand the value of mercy.
He had personally experienced it.
His tragedy was that he wanted mercy to stop with him.
And perhaps this is the question Jesus is placing before us today.
Have you allowed the grace of God to reach your heart without allowing it to change how you treat another human being?
Maybe you've been holding on to hatred because it feels like the last evidence that what happened to you mattered.
If you release the anger, you fear the injustice will disappear.
If you forgive, you fear the offender will win.
If you stop replaying the betrayal, you fear you'll be betraying the younger version of yourself who suffered through it.
But forgiveness does not erase your testimony.
It does not rewrite the facts.
It does not make your suffering insignificant.
The wounds of the risen Christ were not proof that the crucifixion had never happened.
They were evidence that evil had not been given the final word.
And this is the heart of our message.
He does not rewrite history by pretending that sin was harmless.
He rewrites the ending through redemption.
He takes what sin intended for destruction and demonstrates that His grace is greater.
Not every broken relationship will be restored.
Not every offender will repent.
Not every injustice will be resolved in this lifetime.
But in Christ, your suffering does not have to become your identity.
Your bitterness does not have to become your future.
And the person who hurt you does not have to remain the central character in the story of your soul.
Jesus is Lord.
Not your offender.
Not your trauma.
Not your anger.
Jesus.
And if He is truly Lord, then even the most painful rooms of your heart belong to Him.
That does not mean He enters them violently.
It means His Word lovingly confronts what we would rather keep hidden.
Perhaps today, the Holy Spirit is exposing something you've been calling protection when it has slowly become bitterness.
Perhaps you've stopped praying for someone's repentance and started secretly wishing for their destruction.
Perhaps you've been rehearsing imaginary conversations where you finally humiliate the person who humiliated you.
Perhaps you smile in church while quietly hoping someone else will suffer.
And perhaps you've become so accustomed to those thoughts that you no longer recognize what they're doing to your soul.
Hebrews 12:15 warns believers to watch carefully lest a root of bitterness spring up and cause trouble, defiling many.
Bitterness rarely stays confined to one memory.
It can influence how we trust.
How we speak.
How we raise our children.
How we respond to correction.
How we interpret the motives of people who never hurt us.
One person's betrayal can become the lens through which we view everyone else.
And before we know it, we're punishing innocent people for wounds they did not create.
But Jesus offers another way.
Not denial.
Not forced reconciliation.
Not pretending to be healed.
Surrender.
The kind of surrender that says:
"Lord, what they did was wrong."
"Lord, I am still hurting."
"Lord, I need wisdom about boundaries."
"Lord, I want justice to be done."
"But Lord, I do not want hatred to become who I am."
That is not weakness.
That is the beginning of a different kind of courage.
The courage to refuse to become what wounded you.
The courage to tell the truth without surrendering to vengeance.
The courage to obey Christ even while your emotions are still catching up.
And if you cannot yet say, "I have forgiven them," perhaps you can begin by saying, "Jesus, make me willing."
Bring that small, trembling willingness to Him.
Do not manufacture a testimony you do not yet possess.
Do not pretend your healing is complete because other Christians expect you to sound victorious.
God does not need your performance.
He calls you to honesty, repentance, faith, and obedience.
If the pain involves abuse or ongoing danger, seek protection and trustworthy help. A faithful response to Christ never requires hiding abuse or placing yourself or someone else in harm's way.
And if you have been the person who hurt someone else, hear this too.
Do not use this article to demand forgiveness from your victim.
Do not quote Matthew 6 to pressure someone into restoring access to their life.
Do not say, "You're a Christian, so you have to forgive me," while refusing to acknowledge what you've done.
Biblical repentance involves truth.
It involves turning from sin.
It may involve restitution, accountability, accepting consequences, and demonstrating genuine change over time.
You are not entitled to immediate trust simply because you requested forgiveness.
And you cannot use God's grace as permission to continue harming people.
The Gospel humbles the wounded and the offender, though their responsibilities are not identical.
To the wounded, Christ calls for a heart that releases vengeance.
To the offender, Christ calls for repentance.
To both, He offers grace that never makes peace with sin.
And to all who come to Him in faith, He offers something greater than self-improvement.
He offers new life.
Maybe this article has brought a face into your mind.
A name you haven't spoken in years.
A conversation you thought you'd buried.
A hurt you told everyone you were already over.
And maybe you feel resistance rising.
"I don't want to forgive."
Be honest with God about that.
He already knows.
But don't stop there.
Ask Him to change what you cannot change by yourself.
You don't need to feel spiritually impressive.
You need the Savior.
You need the One who died for sinners and rose again.
You need the One who can convict without crushing the repentant.
You need the One whose grace is not an excuse to remain unchanged, but the power that teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to turn away from ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not merely the doorway into the Christian life.
It is the atmosphere in which we learn to obey Christ.
And forgiveness is one of those places where grace must move from something we discuss into something we practice.
Maybe not all at once.
Maybe with tears.
Maybe through many prayers.
Maybe with the support of wise believers, pastors, or qualified counselors.
But genuinely.
And today, perhaps your first step is simply to stop defending the bitterness and start bringing it into the light.
If this message has uncovered a struggle you've been carrying, I want to invite you to respond—not to impress anyone, and not to make a public confession you're uncomfortable sharing.
You don't need to reveal private details or name the person who hurt you. Your story may remind another wounded believer that change is possible through Christ.
And if you have been silently struggling, even a simple prayer shared among fellow believers can become the beginning of an honest conversation.
Because someone reading this needs to know that forgiveness is not always an effortless feeling.
Sometimes it is a long road walked with Jesus.
And nobody should have to pretend that road is easy.
Not because every wound will disappear after one reading.
But because there may come another night when the anger returns, when the memories resurface, and when you need to be reminded of what Scripture actually says.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because someone among your friends may be smiling in public while quietly drowning in resentment, grief, or shame.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus commands forgiveness without commanding them to remain in danger.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is possible.
Someone may need to remember that the cross is still greater than their darkest chapter.
Sometimes a personal message is more appropriate than a public tag.
And there is something else I want to tell you about Gospel Warrior.

Our desire is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, confront sin honestly, discover the riches of grace, and become disciples whose lives are shaped by the Gospel.
These resources are offered to help believers study, pray, mature, and remain grounded in biblical truth.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
More resources.
More Gospel-centered teaching.
More opportunities to reach people who feel too ashamed to enter a church, too wounded to trust again, or too far from God to imagine that grace could still reach them.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. Gospel Warrior is only a ministry seeking to point people to Him.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully—not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your giving belongs under the Lordship of Christ, with wisdom, prayer, and responsibility toward your family, local church, and other legitimate needs.
They're simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who choose to stand with the ministry.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
A growing community that takes the Word of God seriously.
A place where conviction leads us toward repentance rather than despair.
Where grace never becomes permission to sin.
Where biblical truth matters more than popularity.
Where people are encouraged to follow Jesus even when obedience is difficult.
Encourage them to explore Scripture for themselves.
Pray for this ministry.
Help us keep pointing people toward Jesus.
Because the goal is not to build admiration for Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to glorify Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry ever becomes more important than the Savior it proclaims, it has lost its purpose.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought you here.
Can you truly love Jesus while refusing to forgive someone who hurt you?
The biblical answer requires both tenderness and seriousness.
A Christian may genuinely love Jesus while painfully struggling to forgive a devastating wrong.
The presence of that struggle does not automatically prove the absence of saving faith.
But a settled, defiant refusal to forgive—one that knowingly rejects Christ's command and refuses repentance—cannot be treated as compatible with faithful discipleship.
Jesus calls His followers to forgive because they themselves have been forgiven.
He does not promise that obedience will always feel easy.
He does not require us to deny injustice.
He does not command us to trust untrustworthy people.
But He does call us to surrender revenge, put away bitterness, and walk in the mercy we have received.
And perhaps tonight, you will close your eyes and remember what they did.
Perhaps the tears will come again.
Perhaps your heart will still ache.
But this time, instead of rehearsing what you wish you could do to them, you might whisper something different.
"Father, You saw everything."
"You know what happened."
"You know what it cost me."
"I am not calling evil good."
"I am not pretending that I am healed."
"But I do not want this pain to become my master."
"Teach me to forgive as You have forgiven me."
"Give me wisdom to maintain the boundaries I need."
"Lead me in truth."
"Guard my heart from hatred."
"And where I have sinned through bitterness, pride, or revenge, forgive me too."
"In Jesus' name, amen."
You may not wake up tomorrow feeling completely different.
The memories may still be there.
The consequences may still be there.
The work of healing may still be ahead.
But the Lord who began a good work in His people is faithful to carry it forward (Philippians 1:6).
And you can keep coming to Him.
With the same tears.
With the same questions.
With the same honest confession that you need His help.
Because the Christian life was never meant to be a performance of emotional perfection.
It is a life of repentance, faith, obedience, and dependence upon Jesus Christ.
The One who forgave sinners at immeasurable cost is able to teach forgiven sinners how to extend mercy.
Not by making evil disappear.
But by refusing to let evil have the final word.
The person who wounded you may never change—but by the grace of Jesus Christ, their sin does not have to write the ending of your story.
